cards.title: Platform web UI
cards.text: Platform web UI: When you stream runs to a qym platform (`QYM_BASE_URL`, `QYM_API_KEY`), the UI is served by the platform itself at its root URL: - `/` lists your projects; `/projects/<slug>/...` holds a project's runs, datasets, experiments, charts and settings. - `/run/<run id>` opens a run; `/compare` compares runs side by side. - `/docs/...` is the in-app documentation; `/admin/...` is for administrators. - Run pages and comparisons can be downloaded as a single self-contained HTML file that opens offline (the export action on the run page and on Compare). Views keep their filters in the URL, so any page can be shared as a link. The offline viewer below is a separate, smaller tool that needs no platform.

cards.title: Who can open a dataset
cards.text: Who can open a dataset: Every dataset starts open to the whole project: each member can view and modify it. A project manager or admin can restrict one in the dataset's **Access** tab (next to Lineage and Settings; its count shows how many people are listed): choose **Only people listed below**, add project members with the level **View** or **Modify** (the add row sits above the list; each row shows who added the person and when), and press **Save access** (one save for the whole list; the bar stays on screen while the list scrolls, and leaving the tab with unsaved changes asks first). Managers, admins and the dataset's creator always have full access. Switching back to **Everyone in the project** keeps the saved list, and it applies again if you restrict the dataset later. - A restricted dataset is absent from the catalog for people without access; its page answers "You don't have access to this dataset". Its **runs stay listed** with scores, but item inputs, expected outputs, outputs and traces are hidden. - Someone with **View** sees the dataset read-only (a "View only" badge, no edit buttons). **Modify** edits items and versions; slug, production alias, restore, delete and access settings stay with managers and admins. - Any member can launch an experiment on any dataset of the project; the run reads the items with its own dataset read token. - A private test set (admins only) is a separate setting and still applies on top of access.

cards.title: Disable items in a draft
cards.text: Disable items in a draft: In a draft, **Disable item…** (item pane footer or item page) leaves an item out of runs once the draft is published; add an optional reason. The item stays in the draft, shows a **Disabled** badge under the **Disabled** or **All** state filter, and **Enable** brings it back. Published versions are immutable: on one the action reads **Create a draft to disable**. A new draft copies the disabled flags of its parent. SDK runs and downloads use the active items only (`state=active`); **Download JSONL with disabled items** writes all.

cards.title: Filter and edit by metadata
cards.text: Filter and edit by metadata: **Metadata** in the items toolbar filters on a key of the item metadata, including nested keys written as dotted paths up to three levels (`source.region.code`). Up to five keys combine (AND) and are kept in the URL (`meta=path:value`). With a filter, search or label active, **All matching** disables, enables or deletes every matching item of a draft. The confirm dialog shows how many items would change and the first ids before anything is written; deleting more than 50 asks you to type the number. Selected rows offer **Disable N…**, **Enable N** and **Delete N**. API: `POST …/items:batch` (dry run by default), `GET …/items:metadata-facets`.

cards.title: Filter and edit by metadata
cards.text: Filter and edit by metadata: **Keys that hold a list** (for example `tags: ["billing", "refund"]`) are in the key list too, marked `· list`; a key that is a list on some items and a plain value on others is marked `· list or value`. For these keys you choose one or more values and a match mode: **Partial** keeps the items that have at least one of the chosen values, **Full match** keeps the items that have every chosen value (the list may hold more). With one value the mode makes no difference. A list filter shows as one chip, `tags: billing, refund (any)` (any = Partial, all = Full match), and is kept in the URL as repeated `meta` values plus `meta_mode=tags:any` or `meta_mode=tags:all` (without `meta_mode` several values mean all). Up to 20 values per key. In the API `meta=path:value` matches an item whose value at `path` equals it or whose list at `path` contains it; the same shape works in the batch body, where a list filter is `{"meta": {"tags": {"values": ["billing", "refund"], "mode": "any"}}}`. Lists of objects and empty lists are not offered as keys.

cards.title: Local results viewer (offline)
cards.text: Local results viewer (offline): The SDK ships a small browser viewer that needs no platform account and no network. It shows one evaluation: live progress while it runs, or a saved results file.

cards.title: Watch a run while it executes
cards.text: Watch a run while it executes: qym run create --task-file my_task.py --task-function my_task \ --dataset-file data.csv --metrics exact_match --local-ui - The terminal prints `Local viewer: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/` and opens the browser (`--no-open` to skip). Use `--ui-port 8818` to pick the port (default: a free one). - The page streams rows as they finish: a ribbon with one cell per row (green done, red failed, blue running, hollow pending), counts, elapsed time, latency percentiles and mean score per metric. Click a ribbon cell or a table row to read the full input, output and expected text, show a word diff, or copy a value. - When the run ends the page keeps the final state. If you are at a terminal the viewer stays up until Ctrl+C; in scripts and with `--json` it stops when the run ends. - From Python: `EvaluatorConfig(local_ui=True, ui_port=0)` (or `config={"local_ui": True}`), then read `evaluator.local_ui_url`. The viewer lives in your process: keep the script alive to keep serving it. A later run on the same port replaces the earlier viewer. - If `--ui-port` is already taken, a warning is printed to stderr and a free port is used. - `--no-ui` only hides the terminal table; it does not control the browser viewer. Platform streaming (`QYM_API_KEY`) works at the same time.

cards.title: Open a saved results file
cards.text: Open a saved results file: qym ui qym_results/my_task/gpt-4o/2026-10-11/run.csv Opens the file in the same viewer (`.csv` or `.xlsx`; `--port`, `--no-open`). For `.csv` files you can correct a metric score in the row detail: type the new value, press Save. The score is written into the file and the original is kept in an audit column.

cards.title: Search, filter, export
cards.text: Search, filter, export: Search (input, output, expected), status filter, column sorting and the selected row live in the URL (`?q=&status=&sort=&dir=&row=`), so a view can be shared. "Export CSV" downloads the rows currently shown.

cards.title: Building the viewer from a checkout
cards.text: Building the viewer from a checkout: The viewer is a build output (`packages/sdk/qym/_static/ui/`, not committed): cd frontend && npm ci && npm run build:sdk Do this before `pip wheel packages/sdk` so the wheel contains it. For development, `npm run dev:sdk` serves it on port 5808 and proxies `/api` to a local viewer on 8818 (start one with `qym ui FILE --port 8818` or `qym run create ... --local-ui --ui-port 8818`).

cards.title: Latency-sensitive runs
cards.text: Latency-sensitive runs: Tick **Latency-sensitive run** inside the Environments card on the launch home view, or under the name and priority on the first Customize step (it is one setting: ticking it on either page ticks it on both), when the run measures latency. The Evaluation Service then starts the run only when the gateway is quiet, makes other jobs on the environment wait while it runs, and discards and re-queues it if foreign traffic overlaps (up to its limit). Expect a later start.

cards.title: Latency-sensitive runs
cards.text: Latency-sensitive runs: - The experiment page shows a **Latency-sensitive** tag. A job that waits for a quiet gateway reads `deferred ×3 · vllm quiet window` in the Status column; a running job reads `admitted 12:52`; a re-queue shows `↻ 1` and `re-queued ×1 · contaminated`. The Experiments list and the Queue have a **Latency-sensitive only** filter, and the Queue says which environment is held by such a job. - The review pane warns (without blocking) when the environment's schema declares `EVAL_VLLM_POST_RUN_MAX_REQUESTS` and you left it unset: without a ceiling, steady foreign load would be accepted and skew latency. **Set ceiling** jumps to that setting. - Each environment has **Who can launch latency-sensitive runs** (Environment page, Policies): *Anyone in the project* (default) or *Project managers only*. On a managers-only environment a member cannot tick the box (the form says so), and the API answers 403. Project managers and admins change the setting in either direction. - Runs that came from a latency-sensitive experiment carry a small clock tag in the first cell of the Runs page (hover for "Latency-sensitive experiment"); `qym run list --json` has `experiment.latency_sensitive` on each official run. - The flag is fixed at launch; **Duplicate** and **Retry** carry it. It does not change priority or queue order.

cards.title: Evaluation Service versions (read-only)
cards.text: Evaluation Service versions (read-only): The launch form has no versioning box. Under the environments, on the launch home view and on the first Customize step, a **Evaluation Service versions** card shows each environment's current `agent`, `image` and `kb`, read from its Evaluation Service (**Refresh** reads them again). A run records the versions its service reports; nothing typed by a user is stored on a new experiment, Duplicate and Rerun carry none, and `POST .../experiments` answers 422 when a request still sends `versioning_details` (`null` and `{}` are accepted). Experiments and runs created earlier keep their versioning details and still filter by them.

cards.title: Dataset read token
cards.text: Dataset read token: Every launch mints a dataset read token for the experiment. The Evaluation Service uses it to read datasets of the project, private test sets and restricted datasets included, so any member who can launch may name any dataset of the project; people without access to a restricted dataset still see the run's scores, not its item contents. The token is sent only to environments whose schema declares `QYM_DATASET_READ_TOKEN`; for the others the experiment page says the service reads with its own token. It is revoked when the experiment settles and replaced when you retry a job. The launch also tells the service which qym instance to report to: `QYM_BASE_URL` is sent to environments whose schema declares it, so an Evaluation Service shared by several qym instances returns the run to the one that launched it. Both keys are set by the platform; a configuration or preset that sets them itself fails validation until edited. The experiment page shows a **Credentials** row (API key and dataset read token: *active*, *revoked*, *not issued*, *not sent*); no secret is ever shown. In Project settings, API keys, **Dataset read tokens** also lists experiment tokens with an *experiment* tag and a link to the experiment; admins can revoke one by hand (a retry issues a new one).

cards.title: Feedback
cards.text: Feedback: Feedback turns a need into a well-formed request. Open **Feedback** in the sidebar (every signed-in person sees it, in a project or not).

cards.title: Submitting
cards.text: Submitting: 1. **New feedback** asks what the feedback is about: **qym itself** (a need or change for the platform, SDK or CLI) or **a product you evaluate with qym** (pick one of your projects and, if you like, point at one run, experiment or dataset). Then describe the need in your own words, in English or Arabic. Do not paste secrets or customer data: every signed-in person can read a submitted request and its conversation. 2. **The assistant** answers with the questions an administrator would ask later: the business need, who is affected and how often, what you do today, what a good result looks like, any deadline and what is in or out of scope. A checklist beside the chat shows what it knows ("Known", "Partly known", "Not asked yet", "Not known"). It reads the qym documentation (or your project's setup, never its data) and searches existing requests so that duplicates and conflicts are real requests, not guesses. **Enter** sends, **Shift+Enter** starts a new line, **Stop** ends an answer. 3. **The proposal.** When it has enough, the assistant shows a **Proposed request** card: a title, a detailed description, the business need and justification, a **priority** (low, medium, high, critical) and a **complexity** (S a day or two, M about a week, L several weeks, XL a project of its own), each with its reasoning, and related requests marked **Duplicate**, **Conflict** or **Related**.

cards.title: Submitting
cards.text: Submitting: You can change the title, description, priority and complexity (the card keeps showing what the assistant proposed). **Keep talking** continues the conversation; a new message replaces the proposal. Nothing is submitted until you press **Submit request** (or **Submit as a possible duplicate**). Your submitted request keeps the conversation: open its **Conversation** tab to read it.

cards.title: Drafts
cards.text: Drafts: Until you submit, the conversation is a **draft** that only you can see. Drafts are listed above the Feedback list (**Resume**, **Discard**) and are deleted after the number of days an administrator set (30 by default) without activity. Closing the page mid-answer does not lose the answer.

cards.title: Triage (administrators)
cards.text: Triage (administrators): A platform administrator sees a **Triage** panel on every request: set the status (New, Accepted, Planned, Done, Declined), revise priority or complexity, or mark the request as a duplicate of another. A revision, a duplicate link and a decline need a note; a decline reason is shown to everyone. Every change appears in the request's **History** and in the audit log. The list groups confirmed duplicates under their original request.

cards.title: Exporting the list (administrators)
cards.text: Exporting the list (administrators): The **Export** menu in the Feedback list's toolbar downloads the rows that match the current filters (not just the page you see) as **CSV**, **Excel (.xlsx)**, **JSON** or **JSON Lines**. Every format has the same columns: id, title, subject, project, target_kind, target_id, priority, complexity, status, submitter, created_at, confirmed_at, duplicate_of, conflicts (request ids joined by `;`), summary, description, business_need, justification, agent_priority, agent_complexity. Drafts are never exported. Each export is written to the audit log (format, filters and the row count).

cards.title: If the assistant is not set up
cards.text: If the assistant is not set up: An administrator connects an OpenAI-compatible model once under **Admin, Feedback agent**. Until then the list is readable and **New feedback** is disabled.

cards.title: Navigation & roles
cards.text: Navigation & roles: The platform is organized around projects. Pick a project first; its dashboard, runs, datasets, reviews, and settings then stay inside that project boundary.

cards.title: Find your way around
cards.text: Find your way around: | Destination | Use it for | Projects | Open an accessible project or create one when your role permits it. | Dashboard | Read the project's evaluation summary, the daily trend of a task's primary metric on one dataset over the last 7, 30 or 90 days, and recent activity. The range and a task you pick are part of the address (?range=30d&task=…&dataset=…), so a reload or a shared link shows the same trend. | Charts | Track metric and latency trends by task, dataset, version, run, and model. | Runs | Filter, inspect, compare, submit, approve, or delete evaluation runs. | Models | Compare model-level quality, reliability, latency, retries, and trace statistics. | Reviews | Curate root-cause corrections used by AI-assisted analysis. | Datasets | Version test data, publish releases, assign aliases, and trace item history. | Project Settings | Manage project details, members, keys, LLM connections, and project lifecycle. | Docs | Read SDK, platform, CLI, and API guidance without leaving the app. Use the project switcher in the shell to move between projects. Filters, URLs, runs, datasets, keys, and review records remain project-scoped.

cards.title: Roles at a glance
cards.text: Roles at a glance: | Role | What it adds | Project member | Can use the project's dashboards, runs, datasets, reviews, API keys, and LLM connections. Members may modify review data and create keys; a key creator may revoke their own key. Members create datasets and drafts, edit draft items and publish; they delete datasets they created. | Project manager | Adds member and role management, run approval decisions, broader run deletion, key revocation, and project lifecycle controls. For datasets: moves the production alias, changes a dataset's slug, deletes any dataset and restores deleted datasets. | Platform admin | Can access every project, manage platform users and projects, and view or restore deleted runs. Project role and platform role are separate. A platform MEMBER can be a project MANAGER. A platform ADMIN has manager-equivalent access everywhere.

cards.title: Run ownership and approval
cards.text: Run ownership and approval: A run owner can submit a completed, failed, or rejected run and can delete their own run. Submitting asks for confirmation and takes an optional comment. A project manager or platform admin can also submit any run of the project on behalf of its owner (the review history says so), transfer a run to another project member (or all of a member's runs when removing that member), approve or reject a submitted run, reverse that decision, and delete project runs. While a run is submitted or approved its scores are locked: they cannot be edited or reset, and its passes cannot be deleted. A manager rejects or unapproves the run to reopen them. Deleting passes needs the same rights as deleting the run. Deletion is recoverable for a limited time: runs move to Deleted Runs, where platform admins can restore them until retention permanently removes them (30 days after deletion by default). Only platform admins can view that area.

cards.title: Choose the next page
cards.text: Choose the next page: Runs, selection & cohorts explains the runs table, repeat rows, comparisons, and cohort accounting. Run detail & item analysis covers charts, pass views, item columns, and filters. Projects, data & review covers settings, keys, datasets, and corrections.

cards.title: Projects, data & review
cards.text: Projects, data & review: Projects are the platform's access and data boundary. Their settings connect people and automation; datasets define the evidence; reviews turn analysis into reusable corrections.

cards.title: Projects
cards.text: Projects: The Projects page lists projects you can access, with your role and activity summary. Platform admins can create projects. A project manager can also create another project; its creator becomes its first manager. Project Settings contains five areas: | Tab | Purpose | General | Name, slug, description, current role, member count, and status. | Members | Add people and assign MEMBER or MANAGER. Only managers/admins can change membership, and the final manager cannot be removed or demoted. Removing a member revokes their API keys for the project. The removal dialog says how many runs they own in the project (Deleted Runs included) and can transfer all of them to another active member in the same step; without a transfer the runs stay in the project under their name. Each transferred run is recorded with who moved it. While the project is archived, members can be removed but runs are not transferred. | API Keys | Create project-bound Bearer keys, identify them by name/prefix, and revoke eligible keys. | LLM Connections | Add, edit, test, choose a default, or remove providers used by AI-assisted root-cause analysis. | Danger Zone | Admins can archive the project (reversible), unarchive it, or delete it permanently.

cards.title: Projects
cards.text: Projects: Archive hides; Delete removes. Archiving takes the project out of the project list and switcher, stops its API keys and makes it read-only, but deletes nothing. Admins and its members still open it from Admin → Projects or a link: its runs list, run pages, compare, dashboard, charts, models, datasets and settings stay readable under a read-only notice, and nothing can be changed until an admin unarchives it. Auto-analysis and Reviews stay hidden meanwhile. Access can still be taken away: admins and managers revoke API keys and remove members in Project Settings, and an admin can delete the project. Deleted runs of an archived project wait in Trash with their purge paused (Deleted Runs says so); the countdown resumes where it stopped after the unarchive. Runs still in progress lose their remaining results when their keys stop, so the Archive dialog lists them first. Unarchiving asks first and names the API keys that start working again, so you can revoke any of them before the project comes back. Deleting is permanent and removes the project's datasets, API keys, members, LLM connections and analysis settings after you type the project name. A project that still has runs, including runs in Trash, cannot be deleted: its runs must be deleted and then purged from Trash after the deleted-run grace period, which does not count time spent archived. Until then, archive it.

cards.title: API keys
cards.text: API keys: Any project member may create a key. The raw token is shown once; save it immediately. Later lists show only metadata and the first eight-character prefix. A key is fixed to one project, so use a different key for every project and environment. QYM_BASE_URL=https://qym.example.com QYM_API_KEY=<token-shown-once> A key's creator, a project manager, or a platform admin may revoke it. Stored scope labels are informational today and are not enforced; project membership is the security boundary.

cards.title: LLM connections
cards.text: LLM connections: Project members can manage connections used by root-cause analysis. Give each connection a provider, model, endpoint where applicable, and secret key; test it before setting it as default. Secrets are encrypted at rest when the operator has configured the platform encryption key. The analyzer uses the project's default connection, or the first available connection when no default is set. Approved corrections from Reviews provide reusable examples for later analysis. For a repeat run the analyzer first asks which sample (pass) to analyze, and loads only that sample's items. Switching samples with the Sample selector stays on the page; it waits while a background analysis is still running.

cards.title: Datasets
cards.text: Datasets: The dataset catalog is project-scoped. Import CSV or JSONL to create a dataset, then work through its version lifecycle: Create or clone a draft. Add, edit, bulk upsert, or remove items while it is a draft. Publish the nonempty version to make its content immutable. Assign an alias such as production to a published version. Who can do what with a dataset: every project member creates datasets and drafts, edits draft items, publishes drafts and renames a dataset's display name. Moving the production alias (which decides what future evaluations run on) and changing a dataset's slug (which SDK and CI references use) need a project manager; a dataset's creator may still set production on its first publish. Deleting needs the dataset's creator or a project manager. Each delete, restore, display-name change, slug change, publish and production move is recorded with who did it. SDK and CI uploads find a dataset by its current display name or its slug: after a rename, an upload that still uses the old name is refused with an error that names the new one. Controls a member cannot use are disabled and say which role can. Deleting a dataset moves it, with every version, item and history entry, to Deleted datasets (a link in the catalog header). A project manager can restore it there under its original slug; if another dataset took that slug or name meanwhile, rename that one first. Deleted datasets are not purged automatically. Inside a dataset, use:

cards.title: Datasets
cards.text: Datasets: Items for search (it matches item IDs, inputs, expected outputs and metadata values), labels, item editing, revision history, neighboring items, and each item's linked runs. Each row's index is a link: Tab reaches it, Enter opens the item, and it opens in a new tab like any link; Runs for evaluations that used the dataset or selected version; Lineage for version ancestry and change counts, with each version's creation and publish time, and a Change log listing every upload, draft, publish and alias move oldest first, with its time and who made it; and Compare for item-level differences between two versions. Changes are listed in the order they happened, oldest first, each with its time (the head version's creation time when an item has no recorded edit). Each list loads 50 rows at a time (Show more loads the next 50), the first rows open expanded, and the open list stays in the URL. Word changes are highlighted; a field too large to highlight is shown side by side with a note. Download diff saves the complete diff. The version switcher, row menus and the upload wizard work from the keyboard: arrow keys move through versions and menu items, Enter chooses, and Escape closes and returns focus. In the upload wizard each column gets an Import as choice (Input, Expected output, Metadata, Item ID or Ignore). Columns qym does not recognise start as Metadata, so nothing is dropped unless you choose Ignore. Closing the wizard after choosing a file asks before discarding it.

cards.title: Datasets
cards.text: Datasets: Downloads are JSONL. To change published content, create a new draft from that version rather than editing it in place.

cards.title: Reviews and corrections
cards.text: Reviews and corrections: Reviews collects root-cause and solution corrections from manual work and AI analysis. It opens on the queue: the To review tab with the pending corrections, how many are left, and how many of the corrections in view are already reviewed. Switch to Approved, Rejected, or All with the status tabs. Sort the list oldest first, lowest AI confidence first, or most recent first, and filter by source, task, dataset, model, run, confidence, and text. Pending corrections carry a priority tag: High when the AI was under 50% confident, or a reviewer changed a diagnosis it was under 75% sure of; Medium for one weaker signal (under 75% confidence, a changed diagnosis, or a wait of 14 days or more). Hover the tag for its reasons. The list loads 25 corrections at a time and adds more as you scroll. Each card shows a short preview of the input, expected, and output; open it to load the full text and its revision and review history. The Run chip on a card opens the item it is about in that run; on the all-projects Reviews page a Project chip names the project. Filters live in the address (?status=pending&model=…&q=…), so a filtered queue can be shared or bookmarked, and ?id=<review> highlights one review. | Status | Meaning | Pending | Waiting for a human decision. | Approved | Accepted and available as a few-shot example for future analysis. | Rejected | Retained for audit, but excluded from analyzer examples.

cards.title: Reviews and corrections
cards.text: Reviews and corrections: You can edit a correction, approve or reject it with a comment, reset it to pending, or delete it. Approve and reject decide a Pending correction; reset returns an approved or rejected one to Pending, so it can be decided again. Select several corrections for bulk approve, reject, reset, or delete; the confirmation names the tab and filters the selection came from, and the action is refused if a selected correction was edited, removed, or moved to another status (for example by another reviewer) in the meantime. In the All tab a selection can mix statuses: each bulk button shows how many of the selected corrections it acts on, acts only on those, and says how many it skipped; the skipped ones stay selected. Editing an approved correction sends the new text back to Pending: it is reviewed again, and the earlier approval stays in its history.

cards.title: Reviews and corrections
cards.text: Reviews and corrections: Project settings decide who reviews corrections. Who can approve corrections is either all project members (the default) or project managers and admins; it covers approve, reject and reset, single or bulk, on Reviews and on the run page. Require a different reviewer (off by default) keeps the person who wrote a correction from deciding it; an AI diagnosis taken as it is has no human author. When a rule stops you, the buttons are disabled and their tooltip names the rule. A correction decided by its own author is marked Self-approved or Self-rejected. Anyone can still delete a correction they wrote; deleting someone else's needs the right to decide it. Keyboard: j/k move between corrections, a approves and moves to the next, r rejects with a reason, e edits, o opens details, x selects, Shift+A approves the selection, / searches, and ? lists the shortcuts.

cards.title: Deleted runs
cards.text: Deleted runs: Deleting a run is soft-delete: it leaves active views but keeps its data and deletion audit details. Deleted Runs is visible only to platform admins, who can restore a run to its project. Retention permanently removes a deleted run and all its results after a grace period (QYM_DELETED_RUN_GRACE_DAYS, 30 days by default); the page shows each run's purge date and flags runs with fewer than 3 days left. It lists every deleted run, 50 per page, with its project; search by run name or ID, filter by project, and select several runs to restore them at once. Restore stays pinned to the right edge of the table.

cards.title: Run detail & item analysis
cards.text: Run detail & item analysis: Run detail moves from summary to evidence: first the execution context and aggregate behavior, then each item's input, outputs, metric results, trace, and review data.

cards.title: Start with the run header
cards.text: Start with the run header: The header identifies the run, status, owner, task, model, dataset, version, timing, configuration, and execution context. A repeat run also shows its pass count. Available submit, approve, reject, export, and delete actions follow ownership and project-role rules. While the run is RUNNING or PENDING the page follows it: new items and scores appear in place, Runtime counts up, and Live · updated Ns ago beside the status says when it last checked. Filters, the page, opened items and your scroll position stay as they are. Checking pauses while the browser tab is hidden. When the run ends, the page loads it once more and stops. Task, model, owner, and dataset are links: they open the Runs list filtered to that task, model, or owner, and the dataset opens its dataset page (its Runs tab) when the run used a managed dataset version, or the Runs list filtered to the dataset name otherwise. Copy link copies a link to the run as you see it: the pass you are viewing and the item view (filters, search, sort, page, layout, analysis metric and the fields Columns turned off). Export HTML downloads the run as a standalone file.

cards.title: Start with the run header
cards.text: Start with the run header: Under the header actions, the up and down arrows open the previous and next run of the Runs list you came from, in its order and with its filters, search and sort, also across its pages; the count beside them (for example 12 of 140) is this run's place in that list. A run opened from anywhere else, or from a link, steps through the project's Runs list newest first with no filters, and so does a run that is no longer in the list you came from (its count says so on hover). The arrows are links: Tab reaches them, and they are dimmed at the first and last run. The header's Compare with previous opens Compare with the previous finished run of the same task, model and dataset as the baseline, and notes the change in the primary metric between the two run means. It is hidden when there is no earlier run.

cards.title: Move around the page
cards.text: Move around the page: Under the header, a section bar stays at the top while you scroll. It links to each section on the page (Overview, Latency and traces, Deep analysis, Categories, Errors with its error count, and Items with the filtered and total item counts) and underlines the section you are reading. Once the bar sticks it also shows the run name and status, and an arrow back to the top. Filters and Clear sit on the right of the bar because they scope every section, not only the item list; the filter builder drops down under the bar, and Escape or a click outside closes it. When a filter changes, the sections above you re-render without moving the section you are reading.

cards.title: Overview
cards.text: Overview: The overview begins with item, completion, and error counts. A completed run whose items did not all report an outcome (the platform rejected their events) also shows Not received: those items carry that tag instead of a verdict and are left out of the metric means and of Execution success. Metric cards adapt to their type: Boolean metrics show pass/fail rates. Percentage or score metrics show an average and score distribution. Numeric metrics show minimum, average, maximum, and total. Click a distribution segment to filter the items; an empty bar holds no items and does nothing. The Pass and Fail segments of a metric that declares a pass rule, and any Error segment, also take you to the item list, where a banner says what it now holds (for example, "Filtered to 16 items that fail correctness") and offers Clear filter. The overview is filtered too. Deep analysis appears when the run has enough item-level evidence and shows how metrics relate to each other. Filtering, sorting and paging keep you where you are: the sections update in place, and the rows on screen stay (dimmed) until the new ones arrive.

cards.title: Latency and traces
cards.text: Latency and traces: Response time covers each item's run time, without evaluation. Latency distribution leads with the mean, then a track from the fastest to the slowest item with p50, p90 and p95 pinned on it; hover a pin to light the bars holding those items, or click it to filter the page to them. Click a bar, or drag across bars, to filter the page to that range; the range stays drawn over the bars and shows as a chip, and clicking it again clears it. Quality vs latency plots one dot per item for the metric you pick, with the metric's pass line, the median latency, and the fast-and-passing and slow-and-failing corners; a ringed dot is a task error, and clicking a dot opens its item.

cards.title: Latency and traces
cards.text: Latency and traces: Inside the traces comes from the run's spans. Time budget splits an average trace into the agent's work and the evaluation, by kind (LLM, tools, retrieval, other); hover a block for its biggest steps. Under it, one panel per kind the run captured (LLM, Tools, Retrieval, Eval) gives calls per trace, the average call, tokens and tool success; click a number to break it down by call site, tool or evaluator, and Open in Step timings jumps to those rows. A run without LLM or tool spans says so instead. Step timings lists each step, an LLM call site (span name and model) or a tool, with its spread (p5 to p95, the middle half, median and mean), calls and time per trace, and errors. Agent and Eval start collapsed; open them from their row. Find a step or model, group by kind, switch the axis between linear and log, sort by any column, and export the CSV summary, the raw spans CSV, or the plot as SVG.

cards.title: Repeat-run analysis
cards.text: Repeat-run analysis: For samples=k, the repeat section adds a metric picker, pass threshold, group metrics, a pass sweep, accuracy-versus-k analysis, correct-pass distribution, and stability views. A repeat run judges task errors per pass. Each item's value is the mean over its passes: a pass whose task or scorer failed counts as 0, or is left out when lower is better. Which pass failed does not matter, including the last one. | Measure | Interpretation | Pass@k | Capability: at least one of k executions passes. | Pass^k | Reliability: all k executions pass. | Avg@k | Average score across executions. | Max@k | Average of each item's best execution. | Consistency | How often repeated outcomes agree. | Reliability | For items solved at least once, how often attempts solve them. The pass sweep gives each pass's metrics, average and median latency, errors, and completed items. Change the metric or threshold to recompute the pass/fail interpretation without rerunning.

cards.title: Open one pass
cards.text: Open one pass: Click a pass in the Runs expansion or an item's pass heading. The Pass N/k lens replaces every item's reduced values with that pass's output, metrics, latency, status, error, and trace. Use the pass pill to return to the all-pass view.

cards.title: Items
cards.text: Items: Each collapsed item is one row of aligned columns: its number, its Pass/Fail status for the displayed metric, the input, the reason it failed, and its metric values. When the metric values do not fit on one line, the displayed metric comes first and the rest collapse into +N more (hover it for the values); on narrower screens the values move to a second line.

cards.title: Why an item failed
cards.text: Why an item failed: A row that fails the displayed metric shows a one-line reason (hover it for the full text) with its source underneath. The first of these that exists is shown: task error: the item's task failed; its error message. scorer error: the metric raised (status error, failed or timeout). reason: the metric's reason, or an error recorded without an error status (older metrics stored verdict reasons there). explanation: the metric's explanation. label: the metric's label. no reason recorded: the score and what a pass needs, such as "Scored False, pass needs True". Other metadata keys are not read. To get a precise reason, have the metric return reason in its metadata. Search inputs and outputs, sort by index, score, or latency, and use Display to choose the analysis metric, threshold, item metadata columns, and metric-detail fields. Repeat runs also offer Cards and Heatmap layouts. Export the current filtered item set with CSV. The address bar keeps the item view: the filters (bar clicks and the filter builder), search, sort, page, the Cards or Heatmap layout, the analysis metric with its pass threshold and the item and metric fields turned off under Columns. Reload, Back and a copied address open the same view, filtered from the first moment.

cards.title: Why an item failed
cards.text: Why an item failed: To share one item, open it and use Copy link beside its input, or copy the address bar: it names the item you opened (?item=<item id>, plus &pass=N in a pass view). The link opens the run on that item's page, expanded and highlighted. Inputs and outputs show exactly as stored (Raw) by default. Display › Text › Rendered formats markdown in prose while code and SQL stay as stored; the choice is remembered in this browser, and Compare has the same switch.

cards.title: Build precise filters
cards.text: Build precise filters: Open Filters in the section bar, add conditions, and choose whether AND or OR joins them. Groups can be nested. Filter fields include every metric, item categories, approval state, output text, errors, edited metrics, retries, trace errors, and latency. AND — every rule below must match correctness is failed faithfulness ≥ 0.80 Has error false For a metric's passed/failed operator, the run's current threshold is used. Direct comparisons such as >= 0.8 use the value you enter. This makes an AND query across several metrics explicit; adding separate chart filters is not a substitute. AND means the same item must satisfy every condition. Use OR when any condition may qualify the item, and a nested group for combinations such as “failed correctness AND (error OR slow).”

cards.title: Read a classic item
cards.text: Read a classic item: Expand a card to see the full input, expected output, system output, latency, trace, metric strip, metadata, and root-cause fields. A metric row shows its score, opens judge or metric details when recorded, and exposes score editing. Edited values are marked Edited; hover the badge to see who changed the score, when, from which value to which, and the original score. The reset action beside it gives the score back its original value (on a repeat run, resetting the item resets each of its edited passes). Every edit and reset is recorded in the audit log. Scores of a submitted or approved run are locked: a note at the top of the page says so, and a project manager can reject or unapprove the run to reopen them.

cards.title: Compare repeat outputs and variants
cards.text: Compare repeat outputs and variants: A repeat item opens into synchronized pass columns. Each column shows one pass's output, pass/fail verdict for the selected analysis metric, latency, trace, metric values, and edit control. Toggle pass headings to hide or show columns. The output header reports how many distinct variants occurred. Variant identity uses exact output equality after trimming and collapsing whitespace. It is not a semantic or fuzzy match.

cards.title: Per-pass metric explanations
cards.text: Per-pass metric explanations: Click a metric in any pass column to align that metric's recorded explanation or structured metadata beneath the visible columns. If the run did not store pass-specific details, the page says so and shows the run-level metric detail instead. Editing a pass score updates that pass and the run's reduced item score.

cards.title: Cards or heatmap?
cards.text: Cards or heatmap?: | View | Best for | Cards | Reading inputs, outputs, explanations, traces, and root causes. | Heatmap | Scanning repeat-run variance by item and pass; rows show mean, standard deviation, and every pass value.

cards.title: Runs, selection & cohorts
cards.text: Runs, selection & cohorts: The Runs page is the project ledger: filter it to a comparable slice, open a run for evidence, or select whole runs and individual repeat passes for comparison.

cards.title: Read and narrow the table
cards.text: Read and narrow the table: Search runs (press /) finds a run by the name the table shows, its run name, or the start of its run ID. The search is part of the page address, so a reload, the Back button, or a shared link keeps it. The time control limits runs to today, the last 7 or 30 days, or a Range of two dates (both included).

cards.title: Read and narrow the table
cards.text: Read and narrow the table: Use the toolbar to filter by task, dataset and version, model, status, or owner. Columns shows and hides every column: the run columns (run name, status, task, model, dataset, owner, date, analysis, experiment, version, duration), metrics, and system fields. A hidden frozen column leaves no gap: the frozen columns close up around it. With the run name hidden, Select still shows its checkboxes, and unchecking everything keeps the run name so the table is never empty. Its Frozen columns section chooses which of run name, status, task, model, dataset, owner, and date stay in place while the table scrolls sideways: all of them by default. Unfreeze some to see more scores on a narrower screen; the choice is remembered in this browser, and Reset to default freezes them all again. When the frozen columns would take more than about half of the table's width, the rightmost ones (date first, then owner, dataset and so on, never the run name) scroll with the table until the rest fit, and the section names them. Your choice is not changed: a wider window freezes them again. Click a column heading to sort (or Tab to it and press Enter); the run name is a link to its detail page, so middle-click, Open in new tab, and Copy link work as anywhere else.

cards.title: Share or bookmark a view
cards.text: Share or bookmark a view: The search, filters, the time range, the sort, and the page are part of the address: ?q=…&task=…&model=…&dataset=…&status=…&owner=…&range=week&sort=model-asc&page=2 (range is today, week, month for 30 days, or custom with a from date, a to date or both). Copy the URL to send a teammate the same view, bookmark it, or open it in a new tab. A model name alone covers its standard and reasoning variants. Browser Back from a run returns to the same page, sort, and scroll position, and shows the rows you left at once while it refreshes them. Charts and Models keep their filters in the address the same way. A run opened from this list carries the list's search, filters, time range and sort (?list=…), so the up and down arrows in its header step to the previous and next run in this order, across pages. Each row shows workflow status, run identity, task, model, dataset, code version, metric means, latency, owner, date, duration, and available actions. Running repeat evaluations also show current pass progress. A finished run tagged Incomplete completed without all of its data: some items never arrived, or the platform rejected some of its events. Hover the tag for the reason; the run page lists what is missing. An item whose failure event was rejected still counts as a task error when its final attempt failed; an item with no outcome at all shows as Not received and is left out of Execution success and of the means.

cards.title: The numbers above the table
cards.text: The numbers above the table: The top bar (and each project card on Overview) sums the runs in scope: All runs in the project, or Filtered runs while filters are active. Hover a number for its definition. Runs — runs in scope. Execution success — the share of item executions that ran without a task error. A repeat run counts each item once per pass, judged by that pass's last attempt. Metric (scorer) errors do not lower it; they count in runs with errors. An item of a completed run whose outcome never reached the platform (Not received on the run page) is left out. It replaces the older Avg Success, so it can differ from earlier releases. Runs with errors — runs with at least one task or metric error. Models and Items — distinct model names (reasoning and standard variants count once) and items evaluated (a repeat run counts each item once).

cards.title: Expand a repeat row
cards.text: Expand a repeat row: A repeat evaluation is one row marked with its pass count (×k / k passes). It represents one run in which every dataset item was executed k times. Open its chevron to reveal: one member row per completed or active pass, with that pass's metric means, latency, errors, item count, date, and duration; queued pass ranges while a live run is still progressing; best-across-pass highlights where a unique best metric or latency exists; and a Group metrics strip with metric and pass-threshold controls. Click a completed pass row to open the run through a pass lens. That view uses the selected pass's output, score, latency, status, and trace rather than the run's reduced values. The parent row is reduced; member rows are executions. For a repeat run, each item metric on the parent is the mean across stored passes. Expand it when variance matters.

cards.title: Select mode
cards.text: Select mode: Check rows, use the table's select-all checkbox for the current page, or focus a row and press x. The status bar then offers the actions allowed for that selection: | Action | Rule | Compare | Select at least two references. On the Compare page, Copy link copies the comparison with its metric, item filter, winner, search, sort, page, tab, and open item; Export HTML downloads it as a standalone file. Each output's run name opens that item in its run. | Cohort | Lock the current selection as Cohort A, then build an execution-balanced Cohort B. | Submit | Every selected run must be in COMPLETED, FAILED, or REJECTED, and yours unless you are a project manager or admin. A confirmation lists the runs and takes an optional comment; the runs are submitted together in one request, so either all of them are submitted or none is. | Delete | Every selected run must be deletable by you: owner, project manager, or platform admin. | Clear | Leave selection or cancel cohort mode. Esc does the same.

cards.title: Select mode
cards.text: Select mode: The selection, and a locked Cohort A, stay until you clear them: open a run or Compare and come Back, go to another page of the project and return to Runs, or reload, and the same runs are still checked. Each project keeps its own selection in this browser tab. Signing out clears it, with the tab's saved filters, so whoever signs in next in that tab starts clean; a reload keeps it. A run deleted in the meantime drops out of it, and so does a pass reference (checked or in Cohort A) once its run's passes have changed. The pager stays in the status bar next to the selection actions, so you can move between pages with runs selected; in a narrow window it takes a second row there.

cards.title: Select an individual pass
cards.text: Select an individual pass: Expand a repeat row and check a completed pass to create a pass reference. It addresses one execution rather than the whole run and can join a normal comparison or a cohort. The parent checkbox follows the visible scope: collapsed, it selects the repeat run; expanded, it selects all available passes. Selecting the whole run removes its selected pass references, and selecting a pass removes its whole-run reference.

cards.title: Compare runs against a baseline
cards.text: Compare runs against a baseline: Compare opens with one card per run and a Per-Run Averages table. Columns are labelled by model and start date (gpt-4o · Sep 28), or, when every run uses the same model, by the part of the run names they do not share. Hover a heading for the full run name. The table scrolls sideways inside its card with the metric column pinned, so many runs never squeeze it. Baseline — the first run (Cohort A's first run for a cohort) unless you pick another. Every other column shows its change against it on each metric, the mean change over the items both runs scored (so a partial run is not compared on items it never ran): green when better, red when worse (by the metric's declared direction; a metric without one is never colored), muted when the change is within noise. Noise band — ± the 95% band of the mean per-item difference over the items both runs scored. A change inside it is within noise. Hover the change for the p-value and the number of paired items. ↑ / ↓ counts — how many items improved or regressed against the baseline. Click one to show exactly those items in the item list (a banner names the filter; Clear removes it). Each pass / Run average — a repeat run shows one column per pass under its run heading, or one column with the mean over its passes (Avg@k).
